This passage comes from Erasmus' "The Complaint of Peace," and it is a critique of the Reformers and their followers:

"Who ever beheld in their meetings any one of them shedding tears, smiting his breast, or grieving for his sins? ...Confession to the priest is abolished, but now there are very many who never pray at all. ...The solemn prayers of the Church are abolished, but now there are very many who never pray at all. ...I have sometimes seen them returning from their sermons, the countenances of all of them displaying rage, and wonderful ferocity, as though they were animated by the evil spirit. ...Look around on this 'Evangelical' generation, and observe whether amongst them less indulgence is given to luxury, lust, or avarice, than amongst those whom you so detest. Show me any one person who by that Gospel has been reclaimed from drunkenness to sobriety, from fury and passion to meekness, from avarice to liberality, from reviling to well-speaking, from wantonness to modesty. I will show you a great many who have become worse through following it. ...The final paragraph of The Complaint of Peace finishes with the command 'resipiscite,' meaning a voluntary return from madness and unconsciousness: At last! Enough and more than enough blood has been spilled, human blood, and if that were little, even Christian blood. Enough has been squandered in mutual destruction, enough already sacrificed to Orcus and the Furies and to nourish the eyes of the Turks. The comedy is at an end. Finally, after tolerating far too long the miseries of war, repent!"

The passage criticizes the Reformers for abandoning traditional religious practices, such as confession to a priest and the solemn prayers of the Church, and for not showing any signs of repentance or improvement in their behavior. Erasmus argues that the Reformers are actually causing more harm than good, and that they are inciting violence and hatred rather than promoting peace and love. This is also the point where Matthew departs from the Old Testament record. In the Old Testament, Zerubbabel was a hero who led the Jews back from Babylon about 520 BC, governed Judah, and rebuilt the temple. Several times he is called a son of Shealtiel. He appears once in the genealogies in the Book of Chronicles, where his descendants are traced for several generations, but the passage has a number of difficulties. While the Septuagint text here gives his father as Shealtiel, the Masoretic text instead substitutes Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah—both sons of King Jeconiah, according to the passage.
